title: Overlay Two Trees
statement:
You get the roots of two binary trees, a and b. Lay one on top of the other, root on root, and build a single tree:

  • where both trees have a node at the same position, the new node's value is the sum of the two;
  • where only one tree has a node, the new tree uses that node as it is, with everything below it.

Return the root of the overlaid tree. You may reuse nodes of the inputs.

examples.why: Roots: 2 + 5. Left children: 4 + 7. Below that, the left grandchild exists only in b (1) and the right one only in a (3). The root's right child exists only in a.
An empty tree adds nothing: the result is b.
Overlapping nodes stay in the tree even when their sum is 0.

hints: Think about just the two roots. What should the new root be in each case: both present, one present, none present?
If one side is null, the answer for that position is simply the other side, subtree and all. Otherwise the value is the sum and the children are overlays of the children.
That is a three-line recursion: return the other tree if one is null; else add the values and recurse on left with left and right with right.

explain.intuition:
The overlay of two trees is defined by the overlay of their roots and, recursively, of their matching children. That makes it a natural recursion with one shortcut: if one of the two positions is empty, there is nothing to combine, so the other subtree can be reused whole without visiting it.

The shortcut is also why this is fast. You only walk the positions where both trees have a node; everything that hangs off just one tree is attached by a single pointer, like grafting a branch.
steps: If a is null, return b. If b is null, return a.
Make a node with value a.val + b.val (or add into a in place).
Set its left child to the overlay of a.left and b.left.
Set its right child to the overlay of a.right and b.right, and return it.
pitfalls: Stopping at a missing node on one side and dropping the other side's subtree. The subtree must be kept.
Removing nodes whose summed value is 0. Values never decide whether a node exists.
Overlaying left with right by mistake when writing the recursive calls. Positions must match.

complexity.time: O(min(n, m)) positions where both have a node

solutions.title: Recursive overlay
solutions.idea: If one side is empty return the other; otherwise sum the values and overlay the children pairwise.

solutions.title: Iterative, adding into the first tree
solutions.idea: A stack of node pairs. For each pair, add b's value into a, then graft any child that only b has, and push the child pairs that both have.

followups: Build the result without changing or sharing any node of the inputs. What does that cost?
Overlay k trees at once. Is it better to overlay them pairwise or all together?
